prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic angle

statement.case_for: After reading the full set of openings I move my preferred configuration from my own first choice, B016, to B014. Five of eight members place twisted bilayer graphene in their top three, and unlike my IceCube ranking this is support that comes from several independent scientific readings rather than from two members. The substance is what I want the prize to reward: a prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) that a specific twist angle flattens the bands, followed by an experiment (Cao, Jarillo-Herrero and colleagues, 2018) that finds correlated insulators and superconductivity where the theory said to look. That is a clue from nature confirming a concrete idea, and it has been reproduced in many laboratories and extended to other moire systems. The theory-plus-experiment trio is the cleanest allocation anyone on the committee has proposed for any shortlisted candidate.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity of interpretation. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, the phenomenon is sensitive to twist-angle disorder, and the field is less than a decade old, whereas I have said that big ideas can take a very long time to prove themselves. The prize would honour the prediction of flat bands and the discovery of the phases, not an understanding of why the superconductivity occurs. There is also a real attribution problem: Eva Andrei's early STM and transport work on flat bands in twisted graphene is not covered by a three-person cut, and Pearce and others have flagged it. If outside experts say her contribution is decisive rather than supporting, the trio is wrong.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B014 first and argues that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction plus Jarillo-Herrero's 2018 experiment is the cleanest three-person prize, with Andrei's earlier flat-band work a possible but lesser claim.
responses.response: I agree on the structure and have moved toward it, but I would not wave Andrei away. The test I would apply, and ask the outside experts to apply, is whether her STM evidence established the flat-band physics independently of the 2018 transport results, or only corroborated a prediction that was already made. If it is the former, the three-person cut fails and we must reconsider. If it is the latter, the trio holds. I think we are entitled to ask rather than assume.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B016, Halzen alone) first for its observational discovery of a TeV-PeV neutrino flux, while noting that a one-person prize is a narrow reading for collaboration-scale work and ranks twisted bilayer graphene only seventh because the field may not be settled.
responses.response: We share a first choice, so I owe you a plain answer on why I have moved. Your own attribution caveat is the reason: one name for a km3 detector and a large collaboration, with AMANDA and others behind it, is exactly the kind of credit question I would have to resolve with outside reports, and the packet gives us no second or third name. On maturity I disagree with you. The unsettled pairing mechanism does not make the discovery immature; the phases were seen, reproduced and extended. I keep B016 as my first alternative and would support it strongly if the experts supply a defensible credit set.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B046) first as a mature, stable platform, while worrying that the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits already covers much of that ground.
responses.response: I think your own timeliness worry is the decisive point against B046 in this round. The 2025 prize recognised the quantum behaviour of superconducting circuits, and circuit QED is largely a technology built on that foundation, so the committee would be asked to see a new discovery where much of it is a way of reading out and coupling devices. I would be more persuaded if the case were framed around a specific new result from nature, not around the architecture of quantum processors.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks (B013, Katori and Ye) first for a clear, fundamental advance in precision, with independent laboratories confirming it.
responses.response: I take seriously that two names give a clean configuration and the maturity is high, and I do not doubt the engineering. My hesitation is whether the prize would reward a discovery or a measurement capability. Clocks at 1e-18 become a discovery only once they find something: a variation of constants, a dark-matter signal, or a redshift test of a new kind. The 2005 prize for frequency combs and the existing precision-measurement prizes also narrow the novelty. I keep B013 out of my top configuration, but I would not oppose it if the experts argue it is a new regime of measurement physics.

uncertainties: Whether Eva Andrei's flat-band STM work is independent and decisive, which would change the allocation within B014.
Whether the superconducting pairing mechanism in magic-angle graphene needs to be settled before the committee is comfortable.
Whether outside experts can supply a defensible multi-person credit set for B016 beyond Halzen.
Whether B041 would be seen as too close to the 2016 topological prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for these candidates: my work is in string theory, cosmology and black holes, and my connections (Gross, Rubinstein, Van Riet, the Uppsala group) have no stated link to any shortlisted name.
